segments.title: HMS Polyanthus in Q-ship guise
segments.body: HMS Polyanthus is shown in her Q-ship form. She belongs to the Aubrietia class within the wider Flower sloop family.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies HMS Polyanthus, her Aubrietia-class sloop type, and Q-ship form.

segments.summary: HMS Polyanthus appears as an Aubrietia-class Flower sloop in Q-ship disguise.

segments.title: A simple minesweeper built to survive a blast
segments.body: The Flower sloops were originally designed as simple minesweepers, with a single screw and triple-expansion engines. Three hull layers around the bow were intended to limit the damage from a mine explosion. The outer layer could be destroyed while the others remained intact. The magazines were above water and aft, away from a blast at the bow that could otherwise set off the ship's explosives.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the minesweeper role, single screw and triple-expansion engines, three forward hull layers intended to contain mine damage, and above-water magazines located aft.

segments.summary: The Flower sloops combined a straightforward single-screw, triple-expansion layout with protection intended to limit mine damage.

segments.title: From convoy sloop to disguised submarine trap
segments.body: The Flower sloops were reclassified as convoy sloops and then turned into Q-ships. Their resemblance to small merchant ships helped conceal their naval role. They proved particularly successful as Q-ships, using that appearance to disguise their fighting power.

evidence.note: The transcript covers convoy-sloop reclassification, merchant-ship appearance, Q-ship conversion, and their success in that role.

segments.summary: Reclassified as convoy sloops, these Flower vessels could masquerade as small merchant ships and serve as successful Q-ships.

segments.title: Saxifrage survives as HMS President
segments.body: Saxifrage survived long after her Q-ship service. Renamed HMS President in 1922, she was moored as the drill ship for the London Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve (RNVR) unit. She remained in that role until 1988. Restoration under the name Saxifrage was underway at the time of the 2020 recording.

evidence.note: The transcript traces Saxifrage's renaming as HMS President in 1922, moored service as the London RNVR drill ship until 1988, and restoration under her original name at the time of the 2020 recording.

segments.summary: Saxifrage's survival into RNVR service as HMS President traces the First World War sloop type into a much later training role.

segments.title: Speed and the limits of coal endurance
segments.body: The Flower sloops were exceptionally strongly built and designed for about 17.5 knots. They often exceeded that speed in practice. Their 205-ton coal load nevertheless limited their range, so speed alone did not determine how far they could operate.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the ships as exceptionally strong, gives their designed and observed speed, and links the 205-ton coal load to limited range.

segments.summary: Strong construction and better-than-designed speed gave the sloops useful performance, while a 205-ton coal load constrained their range.

segments.title: Guns and depth charges behind the disguise
segments.body: The Flower sloops often carried two 4-inch Mark IV guns. Smaller 3-pounder guns and depth charges supplemented that battery. Combined with the merchant disguise, this armament made the sloops an unexpected threat to submarines.

evidence.note: The transcript lists two 4-inch Mark IV guns, smaller guns, and depth charges, then characterizes the vessels as surprises.

segments.summary: Flower sloops often carried two 4-inch Mark IV guns, 3-pounder guns, and depth charges behind their merchant-ship disguise.

segments.title: Why a small merchant-ship silhouette mattered
segments.body: The sloop combined a strong naval hull with a misleading civilian silhouette. At 1,250 tons, she was substantial but could still resemble a very small, ordinary merchant ship. That appearance encouraged a hunting submarine to read her as a target rather than as an armed threat. Even the unusual paint scheme shown in the video gave little warning of the naval structure and weapons behind the disguise.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the ships' strength, 1,250-ton displacement, merchant appearance, and deceptive paint.

segments.summary: At 1,250 tons and dressed as a small merchant vessel, a Flower Q-ship could look like an unthreatening target to a submarine.
